## Set-up
Our goal is to estimate the incubation period of COVID-19, or, more precisely, the **distribution** of the incubation period.

- What properties of this distribution are especially of interest?
- What are some challenges of obtaining data for the incubation period estimation?


## Set-up

This lecture is a very brief introduction to model-based inference.  Material is based on [The Incubation Period of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) From Publicly Reported Confirmed Cases: Estimation and Application](Incubation%20period%20paper.pdf), Lauer et. al., Annals of Internal Medicine, published online on March 10, 2020. Data and code are publically [available](https://github.com/HopkinsIDD/ncov_incubation).

Please download:

- [nCoV_simple.csv](nCoV_simple.csv): a simplified version of the original dataset; contains the incubation periods of $50$ patients
- [nCoV-IDD-data-dictionary.xlsx](nCoV-IDD-data-dictionary.xlsx): original data
- Code used during today's lecture will be posted [here](../code/L6_code.R)

## Data
- Import `nCov_simple.csv` to R.

```{r, echo=T}
ncov_simple <- read.csv('nCoV_simple.csv')
# or:
# ncov_simple <- read.csv(file.choose())
head(ncov_simple)
```



## Statistical inference
Print some **summary statistics** of the incubation period:
```{r, echo=T}
summary(ncov_simple$incubation)
```

- Does this imply that the true median of incubation period is 4 days?  Does this imply that the true maximum of the incubation period is 11 days?

- **Statistical inference** is the process of making "an educated guess" about the parameters of interest (such as the median), based on data.



## Model-based Inference {.nostretch}
```{r,fig.height=4,fig.width=6}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show code"
hist(ncov_simple$incubation,main='Incubation periods of 50 patients',
     col='lightblue',freq = F,
     xlab='days',nclass=10,cex.main=0.8)
```

We want to model the incubation period with a pre-determined distribution (e.g., Normal) that can be specified by a fixed number of parameters (e.g., mean and variance).   This is called a "parametric" method. 

- Step 1: Choose a model

- Step 2: Estimate parameters of the model



## Estimate parameters
Use R to perform parameter estimation of the chosen model
```{r, echo=T}
library('MASS')  #need to install first, if not installed
result <- fitdistr(ncov_simple$incubation,'normal')
result$estimate
result$sd
result$loglik
```


## Estimate parameters
```{r, echo=T,fig.width=3.5,fig.height=3}
hist(ncov_simple$incubation,
     main='Incubation periods of 50 patients',
     col='lightblue',prob=T,xlab='days',nclass=10)
curve(dnorm(x,mean=result$estimate[1],sd=result$estimate[2]),
      add=T,col='red',lwd=2,lty='dashed')
```


## (Log) likelihood {.nostretch}

- The **likelihood function**, usually written as $L(\mu, \sigma | \textit{data})$, is a function of model parameters.

- Parameter values that "fit the data better" will produce a larger likelihood, or, equivalently, a larger **log-likelihood**. 

```{r,echo=T}
# "Hand calculation" of the log likelihood
log(prod(dnorm(ncov_simple$incubation,mean=8,sd=1.8)))
```

```{r,fig.height=4,fig.width=8}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show code"
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(ncov_simple$incubation,main='normal, mean=4.11, SD=2.32 \n loglikelihood = -112.95',
     col='lightblue',freq = F,
     xlab=NA,nclass=10)
curve(dnorm(x,mean=4.1076,sd=2.3166),
      add=T,col='red',lwd=2,lty='dashed')
hist(ncov_simple$incubation,main='normal, mean=8, SD=1.8 \n loglikelihood = -233.65',
     col='lightblue',freq = F,
     xlab=NA,nclass=10)
curve(dnorm(x,mean=8,sd=1.8),
      add=T,col='red',lwd=2,lty='dashed')
```

- Estimates obtained by **fitdistr** (i.e., 4.1076 and 2.3166 here) are the values that maximize the log-likelihood (called **maximum likelihood estimators**)



## Some other models
These distributions have the correct sample space of $[0, \infty)$ for the incubation period and allow more flexibility in shape (doesn't have to be symmetric)

- Lognormal (in R: `dlnorm`)
- Gamma (in R: `dgamma`)
- Weibull (in R: `dweibull`)

Recall:

- Step 1: Choose a model
- Step 2: Estimate the parameters


## Lognormal {.nostretch}
- Estimate the parameters of the lognormal model

```{r}
result <- fitdistr(ncov_simple$incubation,'lognormal',lower=0.01)
result$estimate
```

- Add the estimated density to histogram

```{r,fig.height=4,fig.width=6}
hist(ncov_simple$incubation,main=NA,
     col='lightblue',prob=T,xlab='days',nclass=10)
curve(dlnorm(x,meanlog=result$estimate[1],sdlog=result$estimate[2]),
      add=T,col='darkgreen',lwd=2,lty='dashed')
```


## Lognormal
- Calculate the log-likelihood

```{r}
# by hand
log(prod(dlnorm(ncov_simple$incubation,
                meanlog=result$estimate[1],sdlog=result$estimate[2])))
# in R
result$loglik
```

- *Based on likelihood*, which model better fits data?  Lognormal or normal?

- In addition, using this model and estimated parameters, we can answer many questions:
  + What is the probability that the incubation period is shorter than 14 days?
  + What is the probability that the incubation period is longer than 5 days?
  + Simulate incubation periods of future patients:

## Discussion on model selection
```{r,fig.height=4,fig.width=6,out.width="0.8\\linewidth",echo=F}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show code"
hist(ncov_simple$incubation,main='Incubation periods of 50 patients',
     col='lightblue',freq = F,
     xlab='days',nclass=10)
curve(dnorm(x,mean=4.1076,sd=2.3166),add=T,col='red',lwd=2,lty='dotted')
curve(dgamma(x,shape=2.61,rate=0.636),add=T,col='purple',lwd=2,lty='solid')
curve(dlnorm(x,meanlog=1.21,sdlog=0.73),add=T,col='darkgreen',lwd=2,lty='dashed')

legend('topright',legend =c('normal','lognormal','gamma'),
       col=c('red','darkgreen','purple'),
       lty=c('dotted','dashed','solid'))
```

- "Modeling is more of an art than a science"
- "All models are wrong; some models are useful"
- Formal statistical procedures exist for model selection:
- People also consider:


## Summary
We want to model a set of data $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$, where $Y_i$ is the incubation period of the ith person.  The models we did in this lecture can be formally written as (using the gamma model as an example):
$$Y_1, \ldots, Y_n \sim (iid) \ \textit{gamma}(\alpha, \beta)$$

We can build more complicated models:

- Bayesian models:
$$Y_1, \ldots, Y_n | \alpha, \beta \sim (iid) \ \textit{gamma}(\alpha, \beta)$$
$$\alpha, \beta \sim \textit{some prior distribution}$$


- Models with **covariates** (e.g. regression):
$$Y_1, \ldots, Y_n \sim f(X_{1i}, X_{2i}) + \epsilon_i$$

- Hierachical models:
$$Y_1, \ldots, Y_n | \theta_1 \ldots \theta_n \sim \textit{lognormal}(\mu_{\theta_i}, \sigma_{\theta_i})$$
$$\theta_1 \ldots \theta_n \sim \textit{normal}(\mu, \sigma)$$
